layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Abstract—The influence of tungsten on the passivity of Fe-29Cr stainless steels was compared quantitatively with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that of molybdenum by examining the effects of these alloying elements on passivation parameters such as the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitting potential

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the primary passivation potential

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the critical anodic current density

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: were determined from anodic polarization responses of the alloys in a chloride or an acid solution. As the content

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of molybdenum and/or tungsten increased, the passive region of the alloys was expanded by increasing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: simultaneously by decreasing both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for the alloys. Quantitative relationships were drawn between the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: passivation parameters and the content of tungsten or molybdenum in the alloys. It was demonstrated that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effects of tungsten on the passivation parameters of the alloys are almost equivalent to those of molybdenum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: when compared on the basis of atomic per cent, a result of the similarities in chemical and electrical properties

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between the two elements. © 1998 Published by Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: INTRODUCTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Ferritic stainless steels such as 29Cr–4Mo alloys, e.g. AL29-4 (Fe–29Cr-4Mo), AL29-4C

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (Fe-29Cr-4Mo-Ti) and AL29-4-2† (Fe-29Cr-4Mo–2Ni), developed by Streicher,' exhibit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an excellent resistance to pitting and stress corrosion in chloride environments together

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with excellent mechanical properties and weldability.2-4 Because of these merits, these alloys

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have been used as tube materials for power plant condensers56 and as heat exchangers for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the extraction of geothermal energy.7 However, intermetallic phases such as the χ and σ

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phases formed during aging at 540–950°C for these alloys cause a serious loss of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: toughness4.7.8 as well as a significant decrease of corrosion resistance.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Recent studies9,1º showed that full or partial replacement of molybdenum by tungsten

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in 22Cr- or 25Cr-base duplex (α + γ) stainless steel delayed the rate of σ-phase formation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and increased the pitting potential of the alloys by a synergistic effect of molybdenum and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tungsten when alloyed at a specific ratio of tungsten to molybdenum. Also, additions of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tungsten to stainless steels,1–-ī3 amorphous alloys'4 and pure iron'⁵ have been reported to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: improve the resistance to pitting corrosion and hence the passivity of such alloys. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reason for employing tungsten as a substitute for molybdenum in the alloy design of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stainless steel is that, in addition to preparing for large fluctuations in the price of molyb-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: denum,1 both tungsten and molybdenum are strong ferrite formers, are in the same column

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the Periodic Table, and thus have similar chemical and electrical properties. However, it

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is difficult to separate the inherent effect of tungsten on the improvement of localized

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corrosion of duplex stainless steels because other factors such as nitrogen and nickel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contents and duplex phases also affect significantly the localized corrosion behavior of these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloys.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The favorable effects of tungsten in improving localized corrosion and reducing the rate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of formation of the σ phase, which were confirmed in duplex stainless steels, are expected

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to be observed in ferritic alloys. Since ferritic alloys such as 29Cr-4Mo are composed of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: single phase and contain extremely low carbon and nitrogen contents, the inherent effect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of tungsten on the localized corrosion of the alloy can be examined and compared with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that of molybdenum. It is important for the alloy design of stainless steels to elucidate the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quantitative difference between molybdenum and tungsten in their improvement effects on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the corrosion resistance of the alloys. The objective of the present study is to examine the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effects of tungsten on the passivity and localized corrosion of Fe-29Cr stainless steels and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to compare them quantitatively with those of molybdenum.
